summary: A satirical news piece describing a fictional 'Zero Poverty' Pact signed on October 17, 2024 by leaders from over 197 nations, promising to eradicate poverty by decade's end through absurd measures like extravagant universal income, castle housing, and a fund powered by good intentions. It lampoons grand political pledges and imagines comic side effects such as toddler-run boards, rock-paper-scissors courts, and obscure celebrities. The piece concludes that the hardest part is keeping a straight face while promising utopia.
one_line: Satirical article mocking a fictional 2024 'Zero Poverty' Pact whose absurd pledges and side effects lampoon grandiose political promises.
key_facts: The 'Zero Poverty' Pact was signed on October 17, 2024, with leaders vowing to eradicate poverty by the end of the decade.
Representatives from over 197 nations gathered at the Gaia Harmony Palace, formerly known as the United Nations Headquarters.
Secretary-General Bartholomeo St. Clair hosted the event via holographic presence and claimed the timing with his birthday bash was 'Pure happenstance'.
Part One proposes a universal basic income dubbed 'Money for Nothing and the Checks for Absolutely Nothing', funded by printing more money.
Part Two, the Housing Inequality Nullification Directive (HIND), guarantees every citizen a castle or at least a five-bedroom penthouse.
The construction industry, not consulted, responded 'Sure, and unicorns will do the plumbing.'
Part Three, the Employment Carousel, promises everyone a job that sparks joy, pays extravagantly and demands very little.
The Infinite Coalescent Fund (ICF) is the financing institution, powered by goodwill and 'good intentions'; critics say it makes taxpayer money vanish.
In the satirical aftermath, board meetings are run by toddlers who decide by the color of macaroni pieces glued to paper.
Schools replace arithmetic and reading with interpretive dance and competitive meditation, and the legal system uses rock-paper-scissors tournaments.
Money loses meaning, so people barter in abstractions, such as potatoes for a compliment or a sports car for a sonnet.
Celebrities become unrecognizable while former paupers become sensations for their 'authentic' poverty stories.
The article states the piece is satire and that the greatest challenge is keeping a straight face while promising castles in the sky.
